questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: The normal magnesium interval printed here is ___ mEq/L.
questions.exp: The chapter uses 1.5–2 mEq/L; units must be checked before comparing numerical values. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: A magnesium result of 1 mmol/L is equivalent to which pair?
questions.exp: Divalent magnesium gives 2 mEq per mmol, and its molar mass gives approximately 2.4 mg/dL per mmol/L. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Magnesium is the ___ most abundant intracellular cation, after ___.
questions.exp: The source ranks intracellular potassium first and magnesium second. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Match the following magnesium absorption entries — 1) Principal intestinal site 2) Net dietary absorption 3) Paracellular share … A) 80–90% B) Ileum C) 30%
questions.exp: The chapter assigns the ileum, 30% net absorption and 80–90% paracellular transport. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Which is the odd one out in the page's ileal-absorption association?
opts: Calcium as the principal jejunal mineral
questions.exp: The source groups magnesium with ileal B12 and bile-acid absorption, while its calcium comparison emphasizes the jejunum. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: The channels named for transcellular intestinal magnesium uptake are ___ and ___.
questions.exp: The source identifies TRPM6/7 for magnesium, unlike TRPV channels used in calcium transport. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: A patient with an inherited thiazide-like salt-wasting phenotype develops hypomagnesemia. Which defect fits the source link?
questions.exp: Gitelman syndrome involves the DCT Na–Cl cotransporter, and thiazides can produce a related magnesium-wasting phenotype. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Match the following renal magnesium shares — 1) TAL 2) PCT 3) DCT … A) 65% B) 25% C) 10%
questions.exp: The table gives TAL 65%, PCT 25% and DCT 10%; do not confuse this order with calcium handling. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Assess renal magnesium transport: I TAL and PCT uptake are described as active/transcellular. II DCT uptake is described as active/transcellular.
questions.exp: These route distinctions explain why the DCT uses regulated magnesium channels while bulk TAL transport follows the paracellular pathway. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: A patient receiving cetuximab develops magnesium wasting. Which pathway is most directly implicated?
opts: Vitamin D activation of TAL ROMK
questions.exp: EGF regulates TRPM6 in the DCT; EGFR blockade by cetuximab interferes with magnesium conservation. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: The TAL paracellular proteins carrying calcium and magnesium are claudin ___ and ___.
questions.exp: The schematic names claudin-16/19; defects can impair renal divalent-cation handling. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Blood calcium rises and activates the TAL calcium-sensing receptor. What direction of calcium reabsorption is shown?
opts: Unchanged reabsorption at every calcium level
questions.exp: The diagram shows high blood calcium activating CaSR, which inhibits calcium reabsorption; TAL salt transport supplies the driving force for paracellular Ca/Mg handling. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Match the following TAL diagram components — 1) NKCC2 2) ROMK 3) ClC-Kb/Barttin … A) Potassium recycling B) Basolateral chloride exit machinery C) Na–K–2Cl entry
questions.exp: NKCC2 and ROMK support the lumen-positive driving force; ClC-Kb and its Barttin partner provide basolateral chloride handling in the figure. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: For Bartter type 1, assess: I The source highlights hypercalciuria. II Its written hypomagnesuria label is a reliable description of a magnesium-wasting mechanism.
questions.exp: The note associates type 1 with hypercalciuria and gives a 20% frequency for a magnesium abnormality, but writes hypomagnesuria. That word means low urinary magnesium and conflicts with magnesium wasting; do not silently equate it with hypomagnesemia. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Match the following DCT diagram labels to roles — 1) EGFR 2) Na/K-ATPase 3) TRPM6/7 … A) Apical magnesium entry B) Basolateral sodium/potassium gradient C) EGF signaling receptor
questions.exp: These labeled components connect growth-factor signaling and basolateral ion gradients to magnesium entry through TRPM channels. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: The DCT figure labels SLC41A1 or CNNM2 near the basolateral ___ pathway.
questions.exp: The figure places these magnesium-handling proteins at the basolateral side, not at the apical TRPM entry site. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
questions.q: Assess the DCT illustration: I Kir4.1/Kir5.1 are shown as basolateral potassium-channel partners. II HNF1B/PCBD1 are presented as regulatory labels, not luminal magnesium pores.
questions.exp: The diagram separates basolateral potassium handling and regulatory factors from TRPM-mediated apical magnesium entry. (Book p892)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Match the following magnesium-lowering drugs — 1) PPI 2) Cisplatin 3) Thiazide … A) Transport-pump inhibition B) Impaired intestinal absorption C) Tubular injury
questions.exp: The page separates intestinal malabsorption from tubular injury and defective transport-pump mechanisms. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: The source orders tubular-injury drug associations as cisplatin > ___ > ___.
questions.exp: Cisplatin, aminoglycosides and calcineurin inhibitors form the printed tubular-injury ranking. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: For the transport-pump subgroup, assess: I PPIs are placed with renal transport-pump inhibitors. II The source ranks thiazides above loop diuretics.
questions.exp: Thiazides > loops appears under transport pumps; PPIs are separately listed under impaired GI absorption. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: A patient with advanced renal failure repeatedly uses magnesium-containing laxatives and becomes lethargic with reduced reflexes. What combination explains the electrolyte risk?
opts: Loss of PTH plus reduced intestinal uptake
questions.exp: Magnesium laxatives/purgatives/enemas increase intake; renal failure reduces clearance and predisposes to hypermagnesemia. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among extracellular magnesium-shift causes listed?
questions.exp: Cell lysis releases magnesium; refeeding instead favors intracellular shifts and depletion. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Match the following hypermagnesemia associations — 1) FHH 2) Addison disease 3) Acromegaly … A) Increased mineral absorption B) CaSR loss with reduced Ca/Mg excretion C) Volume loss with mineral conservation
questions.exp: The page distinguishes CaSR-mediated renal conservation, volume-loss-related conservation and increased absorption. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: During magnesium therapy for pre-eclampsia, deep tendon reflexes become sluggish. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
opts: Assume the drug cannot raise serum magnesium
Diagnose hypomagnesemia from the reflex finding alone
Escalate magnesium solely because reflexes are slower
Consider magnesium accumulation and reassess therapy
questions.exp: Therapeutic magnesium can cause hypermagnesemia; reduced reflexes are a toxicity warning, not an indication for blind escalation. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Match the following source magnesium bands — 1) 4–6 mEq/L 2) 6–10 mEq/L 3) >10 mEq/L … A) Flaccid paralysis/respiratory failure B) Hypotension/bradycardia/depressed reflexes C) Flushing/headache/sluggish reflexes
questions.exp: The table describes progressive toxicity in these ranges, with PTH resistance and hypocalcemia in the 6–10 band. These are approximate teaching bands, not individualized safety limits. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: The source places arrest at >2 mEq/L but flushing/sluggish reflexes at 4–6 mEq/L. What is the most defensible interpretation?
opts: The rows use mg/dL despite the mEq/L column heading
The first row describes ionized and the rest total magnesium
The first row is a validated threshold after renal adjustment
The arrest entry is inconsistent with the severity scale
questions.exp: The >2 entry is internally inconsistent with the rest of the table and the stated normal range. It is flagged rather than silently repaired to an unverified number. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: A patient with marked magnesium excess has hypotension, bradycardia and hypocalcemia. What endocrine mechanism is listed for the calcium change?
questions.exp: The 6–10 mEq/L row links hypermagnesemia with PTH resistance and hypocalcemia. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Evaluate: I This source specifies one diagnostic ECG signature for magnesium excess. II An ECG without that signature excludes toxicity.
questions.exp: The page calls the arrhythmic findings nonspecific; absence of a signature tracing does not rule out toxicity. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Match the following interventions — 1) Severe magnesium excess with CKD 2) Immediate antagonism of magnesium toxicity 3) Search for a cause of refractory low K/Ca … A) IV calcium gluconate B) Dialysis C) Measure magnesium
questions.exp: Dialysis removes magnesium when clearance is impaired, calcium antagonizes acute effects, and magnesium assessment is essential in refractory electrolyte deficits. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Potassium remains low despite replacement in a magnesium-depleted patient. Which channel mechanism explains this?
opts: Activation of NaPi-IIc increases potassium uptake
Blockade of all renal potassium channels
Loss of magnesium inhibition of ROMK promotes K loss
Complete ROMK closure prevents potassium secretion
questions.exp: The source describes a patulous ROMK channel causing renal potassium loss with severe magnesium depletion. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
questions.q: Profound magnesium deficiency lowers calcium by impaired ___ and by ___.
questions.exp: The effect tree shows both reduced PTH secretion and end-organ resistance leading to hypocalcemia. (Book p893)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Match the following deficiency settings — 1) Refeeding 2) Acute pancreatitis 3) Cetuximab … A) Redistribution B) Combined marked Ca/Mg depletion C) EGFR-related renal loss
questions.exp: The page separates intracellular redistribution, pancreatitis-associated low Ca/Mg and drug-related renal loss. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among the listed intracellular redistribution settings for low magnesium?
questions.exp: The source lists DKA, hungry bone and refeeding under redistribution; FHH is linked to reduced renal magnesium excretion. DKA also involves total-body losses, so the label is simplified. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Match the following inherited magnesium defects — 1) Gitelman 2) Bartter type 1 3) Isolated TRPM6-related disease … A) Na–K–2Cl cotransporter B) Magnesium-channel defect C) Na–Cl cotransporter
questions.exp: The chapter connects Gitelman with NCC, Bartter's NKCC2 form with the TAL, and isolated inherited magnesium deficiency with TRPM6. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: A child has hypomagnesemia, nephrocalcinosis and a claudin-16/19 defect. Which urine-calcium pattern is physiologically consistent despite the source's 'hypocalciuria' wording?
opts: Normal calcium excretion in every case
questions.exp: Claudin-16/19 disease is familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. The source's hypocalciuria label conflicts with this mechanism and should be flagged. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: The neuromuscular pathway linked to magnesium-deficiency seizures is increased ___-mediated excitability.
questions.exp: The page associates magnesium deficiency with increased glutamate-mediated excitability and seizures. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: A patient with low magnesium has an unusual ocular movement abnormality. Which finding is specifically listed?
questions.exp: Vertical nystagmus appears in the neuromuscular feature list, alongside seizures. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Match the following hypomagnesemia systems — 1) Cardiac 2) Neuromuscular 3) Musculoskeletal … A) Seizures/nystagmus B) Reduced bone mass C) Tachyarrhythmia/long QT
questions.exp: The symptoms tree connects magnesium deficiency to all three systems, not just a serum laboratory abnormality. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: An ECG in a magnesium-depleted patient shows QT prolongation followed by polymorphic VT. Which rhythm is the key risk highlighted?
questions.exp: The ECG illustration and branch list emphasize long QT, polymorphic VT and torsades. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Assess digitalis interactions: I Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia increase susceptibility to digitalis toxicity. II The source's separate high-K/high-Mg digoxin note means every case of digoxin toxicity has those values.
questions.exp: Low Mg/K are susceptibility factors. Acute severe digoxin poisoning can produce hyperkalemia, but the handwritten high-Mg note is not a universal diagnostic rule. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Which is not included in this page's associated-condition list for magnesium deficiency?
questions.exp: The source lists MI, hypertension, severe low K/Ca, insulin resistance, migraine and colon cancer. Association does not prove magnesium replacement prevents each condition. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: The magnesium intake figure printed for adults is approximately ___ per day.
questions.exp: The page gives 420 mg or about 8.5 mEq/day; dietary requirements vary with age and sex. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: The mild-deficiency entry lists three MgO tablets at 140 mg each. What stated daily total does that arithmetic give?
questions.exp: Three times 140 mg is 420 mg. The source does not clearly distinguish tablet salt mass from elemental magnesium, so check the actual formulation before dosing. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Severe magnesium deficiency is accompanied by ventricular arrhythmia. Which replacement route does the page select?
questions.exp: The severe/arrhythmia branch selects IV MgSO4; oral replacement belongs to mild disease. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Assess the MgSO4 entry: I The scan prints a 1–2 mg loading dose. II That milligram quantity is an appropriate standard adult dose for a life-threatening magnesium-responsive arrhythmia.
questions.exp: The printed milligram loading dose is unsafe to learn as a clinical regimen. Emergency magnesium protocols use gram quantities; infusion timing depends on rhythm and hemodynamic context. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: The source's continuation entry after initial IV magnesium is ___ over the next ___.
questions.exp: The continuation line reads 4 g over 24 hours. This is a source reference, not a substitute for renal-adjusted monitored prescribing. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: Assess replacement follow-up: I Serum normalization always proves full intracellular repletion. II The page advises continuing replacement after serum levels normalize.
questions.exp: Serum normalization can precede restoration of tissue stores, which explains the continuation note; duration still requires clinical monitoring. (Book p894)

questions.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
questions.q: The potassium-sparing agents mentioned as possible adjuncts for magnesium wasting are ___ and ___.
questions.exp: The source names amiloride and triamterene; loop and thiazide agents can instead aggravate magnesium losses. (Book p894)

units.title: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport
units.sec: Magnesium: intestinal and nephron transport · p892
units.guide: Track ileal uptake and TAL-dominant renal handling. Distinguish passive claudin pathways from regulated DCT TRPM6 transport and connect each to inherited defects and drugs. Diagram abbreviations are taught as transport partners, not all as causal mutations.

units.title: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits
units.sec: Magnesium excess, drug effects and refractory deficits · p893
units.guide: Compare drug-related malabsorption, tubular injury and transporter inhibition. Hypermagnesemia depresses reflexes and cardiorespiratory function; profound deficiency causes renal potassium wasting and impaired PTH action. The printed cardiac-arrest threshold is not clinically reliable.

units.title: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment
units.sec: Magnesium deficiency: causes, manifestations and treatment · p894
units.guide: Link redistribution, pancreatitis, drugs and inherited transport defects to neuromuscular and cardiac excitability. Recognize low Mg/K as digitalis risk factors. The source prints an unsafe mg unit for IV MgSO4; do not memorize it as a treatment dose.
